questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. The nurse summarizes the client's admission data. Which findings require follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Correct. Pain that moves from the umbilicus to the RLQ is a classic pattern of appendiceal inflammation.
BP is within normal limits and is reassuring.
Correct. Rebound tenderness shows peritoneal irritation from the inflamed appendix.
A negative hCG helps rule out a pregnancy-related cause of pain; it does not require follow-up.
Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) is a systemic sign of inflammation.
Correct. Leukocytosis with increased bands (a left shift) indicates an acute bacterial inflammatory process.
questions.rationale: Recognizing cues means separating abnormal, clinically significant data from normal or reassuring data. Migrating RLQ pain, rebound tenderness, fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis with bands together point to an acute local inflammatory process that is producing systemic effects. Normal BP, SpO₂, and the negative hCG and urinalysis help rule out competing problems but do not require action.
questions.takeaway: Highlight the abnormal cues that fit a pattern; normal results that rule out alternatives are useful but not 'follow-up' findings.
questions.hintContent: Recall the classic local and systemic signs of acute inflammation and the normal ranges for temperature, heart rate, and WBC.
questions.hintStrategy: Go finding by finding and ask whether it is abnormal or a classic warning sign. Negative tests that rule out other conditions are reassuring, not concerning.
options: Pain that began around the umbilicus and moved to the RLQ
BP 122/76 mm Hg
Rebound tenderness at McBurney point
Urine hCG negative
WBC 14,600/mm³ with 8% bands

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which finding best indicates that the client's local inflammation is producing a systemic response?
optionRationales: Correct. Leukocytosis with a left shift comes from the bone marrow responding to circulating mediators, a systemic response. Fever, tachycardia, and a high CRP are also systemic findings.
Guarding is a local finding at the inflamed site.
Pain with movement reflects local inflammation and irritation near the appendix.
Holding the hip flexed reduces tension on the inflamed area; it is a local finding.
questions.rationale: Local inflammation produces findings at the site: redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired function (guarding and pain with movement). Systemic inflammation produces body-wide effects: fever, leukocytosis with a left shift, tachycardia, and elevated acute-phase reactants such as CRP. The presence of systemic findings tells the nurse the local process is significant.
questions.takeaway: Local = at the site (pain, guarding, swelling); systemic = fever, WBC/bands, CRP, tachycardia.
questions.hintContent: Think about where each finding is generated: at the injured tissue, or by the hypothalamus, bone marrow, or liver responding to circulating mediators.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each finding could be detected by examining only the abdomen, or whether it requires the whole body to respond.
options: WBC 14,600/mm³ with 8% bands
Guarding at McBurney point
Pain worse with coughing and walking
Right hip held flexed while lying still

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which complication is the nurse's priority concern for this client?
questions.rationale: An inflamed, obstructed appendix can become gangrenous and perforate, typically 24–72 hours after symptom onset, spilling contents into the peritoneum. Rebound tenderness shows peritoneal irritation, and fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis show the process is advancing. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin synthesis, so it lowers fever and can make the client look less ill than they are; it does not raise WBC or CRP and does not treat the underlying obstruction.
questions.takeaway: Rebound tenderness plus systemic signs in appendicitis = rising perforation risk; antipyretics can hide fever.
questions.hintContent: Recall the most serious complication of an untreated inflamed appendix and how NSAIDs act on prostaglandins.
questions.hintStrategy: Cross out conditions that the negative test results rule out, then choose the most dangerous complication that the remaining cues support.
options: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with bleeding
Perforation with peritonitis
Acute pyelonephritis
Small bowel obstruction
optionRationales: The negative urine hCG rules out pregnancy, so an ectopic pregnancy is not a concern.

Correct. An inflamed, obstructed appendix can perforate, typically 24–72 hours after symptom onset. Rebound tenderness with fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis shows the process is advancing, and the ibuprofen taken at 0600 may have blunted the recorded temperature.
The urinalysis is negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites, and the client denies urinary symptoms.
The findings point to appendiceal inflammation, and there is no report of abdominal distention or inability to pass stool or gas.

• NPO
  • Lactated Ringer's 125 mL/hr IV

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Orders. The client is awaiting CT results. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a heating pad to the right lower quadrant for comfort
Maintain NPO status and explain the reason to the client
Administer a PRN bisacodyl suppository for the lack of a bowel movement
Administer morphine 2 mg IV as prescribed for severe pain
Maintain the IV infusion of lactated Ringer's at the prescribed rate
Offer clear liquids once ondansetron relieves the nausea
optionRationales: Incorrect. Heat increases blood flow to the inflamed appendix and may hasten rupture.
Correct. The client may need surgery soon; NPO status reduces aspiration risk during anesthesia and avoids stimulating the bowel.
Incorrect. Laxatives and enemas increase peristalsis and intraluminal pressure and can cause an inflamed appendix to perforate.
Correct. Current evidence shows that opioid analgesia does not hide the diagnosis of appendicitis; relieving severe pain is appropriate.
Correct. IV fluids replace losses from vomiting and anorexia while the client is NPO.
Incorrect. The client remains NPO until the surgical plan is known, regardless of nausea control.
questions.rationale: Preoperative care for suspected appendicitis focuses on resting the bowel (NPO), replacing fluids, controlling pain, and avoiding anything that raises pressure in or blood flow to the inflamed appendix. Heat, laxatives, and enemas are contraindicated because they can precipitate perforation. Withholding analgesia to 'preserve the exam' is outdated practice.
questions.takeaway: Suspected appendicitis: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia; no heat, no laxatives, no enemas.
questions.hintContent: Recall what can increase pressure inside, or blood flow to, an inflamed appendix, and what a client needs before possible emergency surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option independently as true or false. Ask whether it could make the appendix more likely to rupture or interfere with surgery.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
0900 (Emergency Department): 22-year-old client with RLQ pain that began periumbilically, anorexia, vomiting ×2, rebound tenderness at McBurney point. Took ibuprofen 400 mg at 0600.

1130: CT confirms acute appendicitis without perforation. Ceftriaxone and metronidazole infused. Admitted to surgical unit; laparoscopic appendectomy scheduled for 1500.

1330: Client states, 'The pain suddenly got a lot better about 30 minutes ago, but now my whole belly hurts.' Abdomen rigid and board-like in all four quadrants; bowel sounds absent. Client is lying motionless with knees drawn up, skin flushed and warm.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• NPO
  • Lactated Ringer's 125 mL/hr IV
  • Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hr PRN severe pain
  • Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 6 hr PRN nausea
  • Laparoscopic appendectomy at 1500

questions.stem: Refer to the updated Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs at 1330. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reassure the client that the sudden relief of pain shows the inflammation is subsiding
Notify the surgeon of the findings immediately using SBAR
Administer the PRN morphine 2 mg IV and reassess in 30 minutes
Place the client flat and supine to relax the abdominal muscles
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sudden relief of appendiceal pain followed by diffuse pain and a rigid abdomen suggests perforation, not improvement. False reassurance delays care.

Correct. A rigid abdomen, absent bowel sounds, rising temperature, tachycardia, and falling BP indicate perforation with peritonitis and a worsening systemic response. The client needs urgent surgical evaluation that only the provider can order.
Incorrect. Analgesia is appropriate, but treating pain before reporting a life-threatening change delays definitive surgical care.
Incorrect. Clients with peritonitis are usually more comfortable with knees flexed; semi-Fowler position helps contain exudate in the pelvis. Positioning is not the first priority.
questions.rationale: The trend from 1130 to 1330 shows a new, life-threatening complication: perforation with peritonitis and worsening systemic inflammation (T 39.1 °C, HR 124, RR 26, BP 96/58). The nurse cannot correct this independently, so the first action is to communicate the change promptly to the surgeon so surgery, fluids, and antibiotics can be escalated. Pain management and positioning follow but do not replace escalation.
questions.takeaway: Sudden pain relief then diffuse, board-like abdomen in appendicitis = perforation; escalate immediately.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a sudden decrease in appendiceal pain followed by generalized abdominal rigidity usually means.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare the vital sign trends. When the client's condition requires a treatment the nurse cannot provide independently, which action gets that treatment started fastest?

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Day of admission: Appendix perforated before surgery. Underwent laparoscopic appendectomy with peritoneal washout. Continues IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole.

Postoperative day 2, 0800: Client ambulated in hallway ×3 yesterday, rates pain 3/10 with movement. Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants; passing flatus. Tolerated clear liquids at breakfast without nausea. Abdomen soft, appropriately tender near port sites. Umbilical port site has erythema extending 3 cm from the incision, is warm and indurated, with cloudy yellow drainage on the dressing. Other two port sites well approximated with no redness.

questions.stem: Refer to the postoperative Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which finding on postoperative day 2 requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
optionRationales: Temperature and heart rate have fallen from POD 1 toward normal, showing the systemic response is improving.
WBC and bands have fallen from 17,900/mm³ and 14% to near normal, showing response to surgery and antibiotics.
Mild pain with movement is expected on POD 2 and has improved.
Correct. Spreading erythema, warmth, induration, and cloudy drainage are local signs of surgical site infection, a common complication after a perforated appendix.
questions.rationale: Evaluating outcomes means comparing current data with earlier data and expected goals. The systemic markers (temperature, HR, WBC, bands, CRP) are trending toward normal and bowel function has returned, all showing response to surgery and antibiotics. The umbilical port site, however, shows local signs of infection, a common complication after a perforated appendix, and needs follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Systemic markers can improve while a local wound infection develops; evaluate each finding separately.
questions.hintContent: Compare each POD 2 value with POD 1 and with normal ranges; recall the local signs of a surgical site infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for trends, not single numbers. One finding may move in a different direction from the others.
options: Temperature 37.4 °C (99.3 °F) and heart rate 86/min
WBC 10,200/mm³ with bands down to 4%
Pain rated 3/10 when walking in the hallway
Umbilical port site erythema with cloudy drainage

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1815: 46-year-old client admitted yesterday with a leg abscess after incision and drainage. Allergy band states 'shellfish.' Family brought in a seafood pasta dish at 1750. Client now reports an itchy, swollen mouth and 'tightness in my throat.' Voice is hoarse. Raised, red wheals over chest, back, and arms. Reports crampy abdominal pain and has vomited once. Audible expiratory wheezes. Client is anxious and states, 'Something is really wrong.' Saline lock in left forearm is patent.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Anaphylaxis protocol: epinephrine 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) IM; may repeat every 5–15 min
  • Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94%
  • 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus for SBP < 90 mm Hg
  • Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV once after epinephrine
  • Activate rapid response team

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Orders. Which action should the nurse take first?
optionRationales: Diphenhydramine is an adjunct given after epinephrine. It relieves hives and itching but does not reverse airway edema or hypotension.

Correct. Hoarseness, throat tightness, wheals, vomiting, wheezing, and hypotension after eating a known allergen are anaphylaxis. IM epinephrine is first-line because it reverses airway edema, bronchospasm, and hypotension, and delay increases mortality.
Oxygen is needed, but it does not stop the mediator-driven airway swelling. Epinephrine comes first.
A fluid bolus supports BP but does not treat the airway. It follows epinephrine.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, systemic, IgE-mediated reaction in which mast-cell mediators cause vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction, and airway edema. The client has involvement of the skin, airway, GI tract, and circulation after eating a known allergen. Immediate IM epinephrine and oxygen address the airway and circulation; response is judged by BP and respiratory status.
questions.takeaway: Known allergen + 2 or more body systems = anaphylaxis; epinephrine IM first, then watch airway and BP.
questions.hintContent: Recall the clinical criteria for anaphylaxis and which medication reverses both airway edema and hypotension.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition first, then choose the one drug that reverses both airway swelling and hypotension.
options: Give diphenhydramine 50 mg IV and reassess in 15 minutes
Give epinephrine 0.5 mg IM into the lateral thigh
Apply oxygen by nonrebreather mask to raise the SpO₂
Start the 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The school nurse is called to the cafeteria for a 14-year-old student with a known peanut allergy who ate a cookie containing peanuts 15 minutes ago. Which findings indicate the student is experiencing anaphylaxis and needs epinephrine now? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: A history of allergies is background information, not a current sign of body-system involvement.
Correct. Spreading hives show skin and mucosal involvement.
Correct. Repeated vomiting after allergen exposure shows GI involvement.
Correct. A hoarse voice suggests airway (laryngeal) swelling.
These vital signs are within normal limits. Epinephrine should not be delayed while waiting for hypotension.
Past inhaler use is history, not a current finding of anaphylaxis.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is likely when, after exposure to a known allergen, two or more body systems are involved: skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, or persistent GI. This student has skin (hives), GI (repeated vomiting), and airway (hoarseness) involvement, so epinephrine should be given immediately even though vital signs are still normal. Waiting for hypotension or low SpO₂ delays treatment and increases the risk of death.
questions.takeaway: Two or more systems after a known allergen = anaphylaxis; do not wait for low BP to give epinephrine.
questions.hintContent: Recall the body systems included in the clinical criteria for anaphylaxis after exposure to a known allergen.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose only current findings that show a body system is involved. History items and normal values do not meet the criteria.
options: History of seasonal allergies
Hives spreading across the chest and neck
Repeated vomiting
Hoarse voice
HR 96/min and BP 110/68 mm Hg
Last used an inhaler 3 days ago

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Pharmacologic Therapy · Corticosteroids
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisone 10 mg daily for 9 months. Which statements by the client at a follow-up visit indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Morning dosing with food matches the natural cortisol rhythm and reduces GI upset.
Correct. Skipping doses after long-term use can cause adrenal insufficiency. Doses must be taken daily and tapered only as prescribed.
Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose, so checking it when symptoms occur is appropriate.
Correct. Long-term steroids cause bone loss without symptoms, so calcium and vitamin D should be continued.
Correct. All providers, including dentists, need to know about steroid therapy because of adrenal suppression and infection risk.
A card that identifies steroid use informs emergency providers and is appropriate.
questions.rationale: Long-term corticosteroid therapy requires consistent daily dosing, gradual tapering, and protection against predictable adverse effects: adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, infection, and fluid retention. Skipping doses, stopping bone-protective supplements, and not informing all providers all put the client at risk.
questions.takeaway: Long-term steroids: never skip or stop suddenly, protect bones, and tell every provider.
questions.hintContent: Recall how long-term glucocorticoids affect the adrenal glands, bone density, glucose, and immunity.
questions.hintStrategy: This item asks for statements showing a NEED for more teaching, so you are looking for unsafe or incorrect statements.
options: “I take my prednisone with breakfast every morning.”
“I skip it for a few days when my joints feel good.”
“I check my blood sugar when I feel extra thirsty.”
“I stopped my calcium and vitamin D because my bones feel fine.”
“I don't need to tell my dentist about the prednisone.”
“I carry a card that says I take a steroid.”

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment (Systemic Signs)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the admission note for an 81-year-old client from an assisted-living facility who has a productive cough. Which findings are systemic signs of inflammation? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: New confusion is important to report in an older adult, but it is not one of the four systemic signs listed in the course.
Correct. A temperature below 36 °C (96.8 °F) is a systemic sign; older adults often show a low temperature instead of a fever.
Correct. HR above 90 is a systemic sign.
Correct. RR above 20 is a systemic sign.
BP is within normal limits and is not one of the systemic signs.
Correct. WBC above 12,000/mm³ is a systemic sign.
questions.rationale: The course lists these systemic signs of inflammation: temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or below 36 °C (96.8 °F), HR above 90, RR above 20, and WBC above 12,000/mm³ or increased bands. This client has all four, including a low temperature, which older adults commonly show instead of a fever. New confusion is also important to report, but it is not one of the four signs.
questions.takeaway: A LOW temperature counts too; older adults often present that way.
questions.hintContent: Recall the four systemic signs of inflammation, including both the high and low temperature cutoffs.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each value against the cutoffs one at a time. Important findings are not always on the list, so match strictly to what the stem asks.
options: New confusion since yesterday
Temperature 35.8 °C (96.4 °F)
HR 102/min
RR 24/min
BP 132/78 mm Hg
WBC 13,800/mm³

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis (Latex)
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse is completing a preoperative interview with a client scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The client states, 'The last time a dentist wore rubber gloves, I broke out in hives and my lips swelled.' Which action is the nurse's priority?
options: Document the reaction as a minor skin sensitivity
Ask the provider to prescribe an antihistamine before surgery
Notify the surgical team and arrange a latex-safe environment
Explain that a skin reaction will not affect the surgery
optionRationales: Incorrect. Hives with lip swelling after latex contact is an allergic reaction with mucosal involvement, not a minor sensitivity.
Incorrect. Premedication does not reliably prevent anaphylaxis; the priority is avoiding exposure.
Correct. Latex is a known trigger of anaphylaxis. Surgery exposes mucous membranes and internal tissues to latex, so the team must prepare a latex-free setting and the allergy must be documented.
Incorrect. Dismissing the reaction could expose the client to a life-threatening reaction during surgery.
questions.rationale: Latex is one of the common triggers of anaphylaxis. A client who developed hives and lip swelling after latex contact should be treated as latex-allergic. Surgery exposes mucous membranes and internal tissues to latex, so prevention through a latex-safe environment is the priority, along with documenting the allergy and the type of reaction.
questions.takeaway: Reaction to rubber gloves → flag the latex allergy and arrange a latex-safe environment.
questions.hintContent: Recall the common triggers of anaphylaxis and how prevention works for a known allergy.
questions.hintStrategy: The best answer protects the client from a future life-threatening exposure rather than treating a reaction after it happens.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis · Client Teaching
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 7-year-old who weighs 24 kg (53 lb) and has a tree-nut allergy how to use a 0.15-mg epinephrine auto-injector. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?
options: 'I can inject it into the outer thigh even through his jeans.'
'If he has hives and keeps vomiting after nuts, I'll give an antihistamine and wait.'
'After I give the injection, I will call 911 right away even if he seems much better.'
'I'll make sure the school nurse keeps two auto-injectors for him at all times.'
optionRationales: Correct understanding. Auto-injectors are designed to be given through clothing into the anterolateral thigh.

Needs teaching. Hives plus persistent vomiting after a known allergen involves two body systems and is anaphylaxis. Epinephrine should be given immediately; antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise.
Correct understanding. EMS is needed because symptoms may recur or worsen and a second dose may be needed.
Correct understanding. Two devices are recommended because about 1 in 10 reactions needs a second dose.
questions.rationale: Delay in giving epinephrine is the major factor in fatal anaphylaxis. Parents must recognize that skin symptoms combined with GI, respiratory, or cardiovascular symptoms after exposure mean anaphylaxis and require epinephrine right away, without waiting to see if an antihistamine works, followed by a call to 911.
questions.takeaway: Epinephrine first, not an antihistamine, when more than one body system is involved.
questions.hintContent: Recall the role of antihistamines compared with epinephrine in anaphylaxis.
questions.hintStrategy: This item is negatively worded: you are looking for the statement that is UNSAFE.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis · Community Response
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: An off-duty nurse at a community picnic sees an adult who was just stung by a bee. The adult has facial swelling, wheezing, and dizziness and is carrying an epinephrine auto-injector. The nurse has directed a bystander to call 911 and has checked the adult's breathing. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Help the adult walk to a shaded area to sit down
Give the adult an oral antihistamine from the first-aid kit
Administer the auto-injector into the adult's outer thigh
Note the time and watch for improvement for 5 to 15 minutes
questions.rationale: The nurse activates help and assesses the airway first so that EMS is on the way while care begins. Epinephrine is given as soon as anaphylaxis is recognized because delay increases mortality. The client is then positioned to support venous return and prevent collapse (a position of comfort if breathing is difficult). Timing the dose allows a second dose if symptoms persist, and the hand-off to EMS ensures continuity of care.
questions.takeaway: Call for help, epinephrine, position, time and monitor, hand off.
questions.hintContent: Recall why the timing of epinephrine is linked to survival and why clients should not stand or walk during anaphylaxis.
questions.hintStrategy: Help is on the way and breathing has been checked. Choose the step that treats the life threat.
optionRationales: A client with anaphylaxis should not stand or walk, because a sudden position change can cause collapse. The adult should lie down with the legs elevated after epinephrine.
Antihistamines act slowly and do not reverse airway swelling or hypotension. They never replace epinephrine.
Correct. Epinephrine is given as soon as anaphylaxis is recognized because delay increases mortality.
The time is noted after the injection so a second dose can be timed. Watching without treating delays care.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis · Prioritization
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit receives four client updates at the same time. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with rheumatoid arthritis who reports 90 minutes of morning stiffness in both hands and wrists today
A client with cellulitis who has a temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) on day 1 of IV antibiotics
A client taking prednisone 40 mg daily whose fasting blood glucose this morning is 168 mg/dL
A client with a peanut allergy who has an itchy throat and hoarse voice after a visitor's snack
optionRationales: Incorrect. Prolonged morning stiffness is expected in active RA and is not an immediate threat.
Incorrect. Low-grade fever on day 1 of antibiotics for cellulitis is expected while therapy takes effect.
Incorrect. Steroid-induced hyperglycemia needs follow-up, but it is not an immediate life threat.
Correct. Throat itching and hoarseness after possible exposure to a known allergen suggest airway involvement in early anaphylaxis, which can progress to airway obstruction within minutes.
questions.rationale: Prioritization follows ABCs and the principle that acute, unstable problems come before expected or chronic findings. A hoarse voice after possible allergen exposure signals laryngeal edema, an airway threat. The other clients have findings that are expected or that require follow-up but are not immediately life-threatening.
questions.takeaway: New hoarseness after allergen exposure is an airway emergency; see that client first.
questions.hintContent: Recall which body system is threatened first in severe allergic reactions and how fast it can progress.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which findings are expected for each client's condition. The priority is the one that is unexpected AND threatens airway, breathing, or circulation.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Anaphylaxis · Discharge Planning
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: An adult client is being discharged after treatment for anaphylaxis caused by shellfish. Which instructions should the nurse include in the discharge teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Carry two epinephrine auto-injectors at all times
Store the auto-injector in the car's glove compartment so it is always available
Wear a medical alert bracelet or necklace that identifies the allergy
Take an antihistamine at the first symptom and use epinephrine only if it does not work
Follow the written anaphylaxis emergency action plan
Schedule a follow-up appointment with an allergist
optionRationales: Correct. A second dose is needed in some reactions, and a device can misfire.
Incorrect. Extreme heat and cold degrade epinephrine; store it at room temperature and keep it with the client.
Correct. Medical identification speeds recognition and treatment if the client cannot speak.
Incorrect. Antihistamines do not treat airway edema or shock; waiting delays epinephrine.
Correct. A written plan tells the client and others when and how to use epinephrine.
Correct. An allergist confirms triggers, provides avoidance education, and evaluates long-term management.
questions.rationale: Discharge after anaphylaxis focuses on avoidance, rapid recognition, and immediate self-treatment. Clients should carry two auto-injectors stored at room temperature, wear medical identification, follow a written action plan, and see an allergist. Relying on antihistamines instead of epinephrine is a dangerous misconception.
questions.takeaway: Two auto-injectors, ID, action plan, allergist; epinephrine is never replaced by an antihistamine.
questions.hintContent: Recall how temperature affects epinephrine and why a second dose may be needed.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option as its own true/false statement. Look for common but dangerous misconceptions.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Diagnostic Tests (ESR and CRP)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is on day 5 of IV antibiotics for an infected leg wound. The CRP has decreased from 12.4 mg/dL on admission to 3.1 mg/dL. The ESR has changed from 72 mm/hr to 68 mm/hr. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: CRP is a protein made by the liver that rises with inflammation and falls quickly once it is controlled, which makes it useful for monitoring response to treatment. ESR is nonspecific and changes slowly, so it may stay elevated for weeks. A falling CRP with a slowly changing ESR is consistent with effective therapy.
questions.takeaway: CRP changes fast and tracks treatment; ESR lags behind.
questions.hintContent: Compare how quickly CRP and ESR respond to the start and end of inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Two markers are moving at different speeds. Decide what each trend means before choosing the explanation.
options: The small ESR change shows the antibiotics are not working
The CRP shows a response; the ESR is slow to change
The results conflict, so a laboratory error is likely
The falling CRP with a high ESR signals a new infection
optionRationales: ESR is nonspecific and changes slowly, so a small change after 5 days does not mean treatment has failed.
Correct. CRP rises and falls quickly with inflammation, so a falling CRP shows response to treatment, while the ESR may stay elevated for weeks.
The two markers normally change at different speeds, so the pattern does not suggest an error.
A new infection would make the CRP rise, not fall.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment · Local Inflammation vs Infection
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client's abdominal incision on postoperative day 2 after an open colectomy for ulcerative colitis. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: Narrow pink edges along an approximated incision are a normal inflammatory response.
Scant serosanguineous drainage is expected early in healing.
Correct. A red streak extending from the incision suggests spreading infection.
Correct. Thick, cloudy, foul-smelling drainage is purulent and suggests infection.
Mild tenderness around the incision is expected on postoperative day 2.
questions.rationale: Every surgical wound shows a normal inflammatory response: mild redness at the edges, some swelling, tenderness, and serous or serosanguineous drainage. Findings that spread beyond the wound, increase over time, or involve purulent drainage suggest infection. Recognizing the difference prevents both over-reporting expected findings and missing early infection.
questions.takeaway: Narrow pink edges and scant serosanguineous drainage are normal; streaking and pus are not.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal appearance of a healing wound and the local signs that suggest infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each finding is limited to the wound edge and mild, or spreading and changing in character.
options: Pink edges extending 2 mm from the approximated incision
Scant serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
Red streak extending 5 cm from the incision toward the flank
Thick, cloudy drainage with a foul odor
Mild tenderness around the incision

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Diagnostic Tests · Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with joint pain, fatigue, and a rash over the cheeks is being evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus. Her ESR is 58 mm/hr. Which serum protein electrophoresis result should the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: The normal ESR for a woman is about 0–20 mm/hr, so 58 mm/hr indicates active inflammation. In SLE, B cells produce large amounts of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins), increasing the gamma globulin fraction, while albumin often falls with chronic inflammation or renal loss. These nonspecific tests support the diagnosis alongside specific tests such as ANA.
questions.takeaway: SLE: high ESR, high gamma globulin, low albumin.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal ESR range for women and which protein fraction contains antibodies.
questions.hintStrategy: Confirm that the ESR is elevated for a woman, then think about what an autoimmune disease produces in excess.
options: Decreased gamma globulin with increased albumin
Normal protein fractions
Decreased gamma globulin and albumin
Increased gamma globulin, decreased albumin
optionRationales: Autoantibody production raises, not lowers, gamma globulin, and albumin tends to fall with chronic inflammation.
Active autoimmune inflammation, reflected by an ESR of 58 mm/hr (normal for a woman is about 0–20 mm/hr), changes the protein fractions.
Albumin may fall, but gamma globulin rises because B cells produce large amounts of autoantibodies.
Correct. In SLE, B cells produce large amounts of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins), which increases the gamma globulin fraction, while albumin often falls with chronic inflammation or renal loss.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Diagnostic Tests (Prioritizing Results)
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse reviews morning laboratory results for four clients. Which result should the nurse report to the provider first?
options: A client with rheumatoid arthritis whose ESR is 24 mm/hr, down from 40 mm/hr last month
A client with a healing leg wound whose WBC fell from 13,000 to 9,400/mm³
A client with pneumonia: T 35.7 °C (96.3 °F), HR 118, RR 28, WBC 14,800/mm³ with 18% bands
A client with lupus whose serum protein electrophoresis shows increased gamma globulin and decreased albumin
optionRationales: Incorrect. A falling ESR shows the chronic inflammation is improving; it does not need urgent action.
Incorrect. A WBC falling into the normal range shows the infection is resolving.

Correct. A temperature below 36 °C, HR above 90, RR above 20, and a high WBC with many bands are all four systemic signs of inflammation in a client with a known infection. This is unstable and needs prompt reporting.
Incorrect. Increased gamma globulin is an expected finding in SLE and is not an acute threat.
questions.rationale: The nurse interprets each result in context. The client with pneumonia has all four systemic signs of inflammation, including a low temperature, which shows the infection is no longer local and the client is unstable. The other results are improving or are expected for the client's chronic condition.
questions.takeaway: Report systemic signs first; a LOW temperature counts too.
questions.hintContent: Recall the systemic signs of inflammation and the expected serum protein electrophoresis finding in SLE.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which result is unexpected for that client's situation AND suggests an acute threat.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Pharmacologic Therapy · Salicylates
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client has been taking high-dose aspirin for arthritis pain and was recently started on another over-the-counter product that also contains aspirin. Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of salicylate toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Ringing in the ears
Rapid, deep breathing
Pinpoint pupils
New confusion
Nausea and vomiting
Heart rate of 48/min
optionRationales: Correct. Tinnitus and decreased hearing are early signs of salicylism.
Correct. Salicylates stimulate the breathing center, causing rapid, deep breathing.
Incorrect. Pinpoint pupils suggest opioid toxicity, not salicylate toxicity.
Correct. Confusion and agitation indicate CNS toxicity, which can occur at lower levels in older adults.
Correct. GI irritation and stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone cause nausea and vomiting.
Incorrect. Salicylate toxicity typically causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.
questions.rationale: Salicylism presents with tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, vomiting, hyperventilation, sweating, and confusion. Older adults are at particular risk because of reduced renal clearance and because many combination OTC products contain aspirin. The nurse should hold the aspirin, notify the provider, and review all OTC products.
questions.takeaway: Tinnitus + hyperventilation + confusion in a client on aspirin = check for salicylate toxicity.
questions.hintContent: Recall the effects of salicylates on the ear, the respiratory center, and the GI tract.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option separately. Watch for findings that belong to a different drug's toxicity.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Pharmacologic Therapy · Non-opioid Analgesics
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with acute bursitis of the elbow has been taking ibuprofen and asks, 'Can I switch to acetaminophen? My neighbor says it works the same on the swelling.' Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: 'Acetaminophen reduces pain and fever but has little effect on swelling.'
'Acetaminophen reduces swelling better and is much easier on the stomach.'
'Acetaminophen and ibuprofen work the same way, so either is fine.'
'Acetaminophen is an NSAID, so it has the same benefits and risks.'
optionRationales: Correct. Acetaminophen acts mainly in the central nervous system; it is analgesic and antipyretic but has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen is gentler on the stomach but does not reduce swelling better than an NSAID.
Incorrect. The drugs have different mechanisms; ibuprofen inhibits COX enzymes peripherally at the site of inflammation.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen is not an NSAID; its major risk is liver toxicity, not GI bleeding.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs reduce inflammation by blocking prostaglandin synthesis at the site of injury, which lowers swelling, pain, and fever. Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever through central effects but does not meaningfully reduce inflammation. The client should know that switching may relieve pain but not swelling, and should not exceed the maximum daily acetaminophen dose.
questions.takeaway: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever, not inflammation.
questions.hintContent: Recall where acetaminophen acts compared with NSAIDs.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what the client is really asking about (swelling) and choose the answer that addresses that effect accurately.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Pharmacologic Therapy · NSAID Safety
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client is prescribed ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours for acute tendinitis. Which item in the client's medication history is most important for the nurse to clarify with the prescriber before giving the first dose?
options: Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily
Loratadine 10 mg daily in spring
Warfarin 5 mg daily
Vitamin D 1,000 units daily
optionRationales: Incorrect. Levothyroxine has no clinically important interaction with ibuprofen.
Incorrect. Loratadine does not interact significantly with NSAIDs.
Correct. NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and irritate the GI mucosa; combined with warfarin, they substantially increase the risk of serious bleeding.
Incorrect. Vitamin D does not increase NSAID risks.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs reversibly inhibit platelet aggregation and can cause GI ulceration. Combined with an anticoagulant such as warfarin, the risk of GI bleeding rises considerably. The nurse should hold the dose and clarify the order; acetaminophen or a topical agent may be a safer alternative.
questions.takeaway: NSAID + anticoagulant = major bleeding risk; clarify before giving.
questions.hintContent: Recall the effects of NSAIDs on platelets and the stomach lining.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the medication whose adverse effect would add to an NSAID's most dangerous adverse effect.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Pharmacologic Therapy · NSAID Contraindications
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing prescriptions for an oral NSAID written for several clients. For which clients should the nurse question the prescription? Select all that apply.
optionRationales: An NSAID is appropriate for acute inflammation from a sprain in a healthy adult.
Correct. NSAIDs impair platelet function and irritate the stomach lining, which increases bleeding risk with warfarin.
Correct. NSAIDs reduce kidney blood flow and can worsen advanced chronic kidney disease.
NSAIDs are effective for prostaglandin-mediated menstrual pain.
Correct. NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining and can worsen an active ulcer.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs are effective for acute inflammation and prostaglandin-mediated pain, but their effects on the stomach lining, kidneys, and bleeding create important cautions. Clients with active GI bleeding, advanced kidney disease, or anticoagulant therapy need the prescription questioned.
questions.takeaway: Question NSAIDs with active GI bleeding, advanced kidney disease, or anticoagulants.
questions.hintContent: Recall the organ systems affected when NSAIDs block prostaglandins and the drug interactions that increase bleeding.
questions.hintStrategy: For each client, ask whether the condition involves an organ that NSAIDs can harm.
options: A 25-year-old with an ankle sprain and no medical history
A client who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation
A client with chronic kidney disease and an eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73 m²
A 32-year-old with primary dysmenorrhea
A client with a bleeding duodenal ulcer diagnosed last week

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Pharmacologic Therapy · Corticosteroids
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client who takes prednisone 30 mg daily for Crohn's disease is on postoperative day 4 after a bowel resection. The client reports increasing incisional pain. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), HR is 98, and the incision has slight swelling without redness. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: The findings are within expected limits for postoperative day 4
The prednisone has fully controlled the inflammatory response
Slight swelling without redness rules out a wound infection
The prednisone may be masking signs of a developing infection
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pain should be decreasing, not increasing, by day 4; together with low-grade fever and tachycardia, this is a change from the expected course.
Incorrect. Corticosteroids suppress the visible response but do not remove the underlying process.
Incorrect. Corticosteroids reduce redness and swelling, so their absence does not rule out infection.

Correct. Corticosteroids suppress fever, redness, and swelling. Subtle findings such as increasing pain, a low-grade temperature, and tachycardia may be the only signs of infection and should be reported.
questions.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress the immune response and many inflammatory mediators, reducing fever and the classic local signs. Clients on high-dose or long-term therapy can therefore have serious infections with only subtle findings. The nurse compares findings with the expected recovery course and reports changes early.
questions.takeaway: Steroids hide the classic signs of infection; subtle changes matter.
questions.hintContent: Recall what corticosteroids do to fever, redness, and swelling.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare the findings with what is expected on day 4, and then ask how the client's medication could change how an infection looks.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Independent Interventions · Heat and Cold
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis reports stiffness in the hands lasting about an hour each morning. There is no acute redness or warmth over the joints. Which intervention should the nurse suggest?
options: Apply ice packs to both hands for 60 minutes right after waking up
Keep the hands immobilized in splints all day
Take a warm shower or soak the hands in warm water after waking
Delay all hand activity until the afternoon
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cold is more useful for acute, hot, swollen joints, and 60 minutes of cold risks tissue injury.
Incorrect. Continuous immobilization increases stiffness and weakness; splints are used selectively, often at night.
Correct. Moist heat increases blood flow and tissue elasticity, relieving chronic joint stiffness.
Incorrect. Avoiding activity worsens stiffness; gentle range-of-motion exercises after heat are encouraged.
questions.rationale: Heat is generally used for chronic stiffness and muscle spasm because it promotes circulation and relaxation. Cold is used for acute inflammation to reduce swelling and pain. Warm morning showers or soaks followed by gentle range-of-motion exercises help clients with RA maintain function.
questions.takeaway: Heat for chronic stiffness; cold for acute swelling.
questions.hintContent: Recall the physiological effects of heat compared with cold on blood flow and tissue elasticity.
questions.hintStrategy: Note whether the stem describes an acute flare or chronic stiffness, then match the therapy.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Surgery (Cholecystectomy)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client admitted with acute cholecystitis is NPO and awaiting cholecystectomy. The client says, 'I'm starving. Why can't I just have a little something to eat?' Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: 'Eating causes your gallbladder to contract, which increases the inflammation and pain.'
'You need to stay NPO so the surgeon can see your stomach and bowel clearly on the x-ray tomorrow.'
'Food will neutralize the antibiotics you're receiving.'
'Not eating will help you lose weight, which is important before surgery.'
optionRationales: Correct. Food, especially fat, triggers cholecystokinin release, which makes the inflamed gallbladder contract against an obstruction and worsens pain.
Incorrect. NPO status is not primarily for imaging of the stomach in this case.
Incorrect. Food does not neutralize IV antibiotics.
Incorrect. Weight loss is not the purpose of NPO status and should not be implied.
questions.rationale: In acute cholecystitis, resting the inflamed organ is a key intervention. Eating stimulates cholecystokinin, causing gallbladder contraction and increasing pain and inflammation. NPO status also prepares the client for surgery. The nurse should explain this clearly and provide IV fluids, analgesia, and mouth care for comfort.
questions.takeaway: Rest the inflamed gallbladder: NPO prevents CCK-driven contraction.
questions.hintContent: Recall which hormone is released when food enters the duodenum and what it does to the gallbladder.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that is physiologically accurate and directly answers the client's 'why.'

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Lifespan Considerations · Children
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 14-month-old who weighs 10 kg (22 lb) has had acute gastroenteritis with diarrhea for 2 days. The parent reports only two wet diapers today. The child is alert, with moist mucous membranes. Which intervention is the nurse's priority?
questions.rationale: Infants and young children have a higher proportion of body water, a higher metabolic rate, and immature kidneys that cannot concentrate urine well, so fluid losses from inflammation of the GI tract quickly lead to dehydration. Mild to moderate dehydration is treated with small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution. Urine output (wet diapers) is an easy and reliable indicator of hydration.
questions.takeaway: Children dehydrate fast; small, frequent ORS and count the wet diapers.
questions.hintContent: Recall how body water, metabolic rate, and kidney maturity differ between young children and adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider why fluid loss is more dangerous in a young child, then choose the intervention that safely replaces fluid and electrolytes.
options: Offer undiluted apple juice to replace the lost fluids
Give an over-the-counter antidiarrheal medication
Give small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution
Withhold all fluids for 24 hours to rest the bowel
optionRationales: Undiluted juice is high in sugar, can worsen diarrhea, and does not replace electrolytes.
Antidiarrheal drugs are not recommended for young children and do not correct fluid loss.

Correct. Fluid losses are a larger proportion of a young child's total body water, so dehydration develops quickly. Mild to moderate dehydration is treated with small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution, and effectiveness is judged by counting wet diapers.
Withholding fluids would rapidly worsen dehydration in a young child.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Independent Interventions · Psychosocial Support
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 15-year-old with Crohn's disease has been taking prednisone for 6 weeks and tells the nurse, 'I'm going to stop taking it. My face is so round and I have acne. Everyone at school stares at me.' Which response by the nurse is best?
options: 'Your health is much more important than how you look right now, so keep taking it.'
'Tell me more about how these changes are affecting you at school.'
'Lots of teenagers have acne, so no one will notice.'
'You can stop the prednisone once your symptoms are better.'
optionRationales: Incorrect. This dismisses the adolescent's feelings and is likely to reduce adherence.

Correct. Exploring the client's feelings shows respect for the developmental importance of body image and peer acceptance. It opens a discussion about the temporary nature of the changes and the danger of stopping abruptly.
Incorrect. False reassurance minimizes the concern and closes communication.
Incorrect. Stopping prednisone abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency; it must be tapered as prescribed.
questions.rationale: Body image and peer acceptance are central developmental concerns in adolescence, and visible corticosteroid adverse effects are a common reason teens stop treatment. A therapeutic, open-ended response encourages the client to express feelings, allowing the nurse to address misconceptions, explain that the changes usually resolve after tapering, and involve the provider in problem-solving.
questions.takeaway: With adolescents, explore body-image concerns first; adherence follows trust.
questions.hintContent: Recall the developmental priorities of adolescence and the principles of therapeutic communication.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that dismiss feelings, give false reassurance, or give unsafe advice.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Collaborative Therapies · Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and frailty has a persistently elevated CRP with no acute illness. Which collaborative interventions should the nurse anticipate to reduce the client's chronic inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Referral to physical therapy for a progressive resistance training program
Bed rest to conserve the client's energy
Referral to a dietitian for an anti-inflammatory eating plan rich in vegetables, fish, and whole grains
Daily high-dose NSAIDs to lower the CRP level
Support for improved control of blood glucose
A high-saturated-fat diet to prevent muscle loss
optionRationales: Correct. Resistance training improves strength and mobility and has been shown to lower inflammatory markers in older adults.
Incorrect. Inactivity worsens frailty and muscle loss and is associated with higher inflammation.
Correct. A Mediterranean-style diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains reduces inflammatory markers.
Incorrect. Long-term NSAIDs carry GI, renal, and cardiovascular risks, especially in older adults, and are not used to treat a lab value.
Correct. Controlling diabetes is a modifiable factor that reduces chronic inflammation.
Incorrect. Saturated fats promote inflammation; protein, not saturated fat, supports muscle mass.
questions.rationale: Chronic low-grade inflammation in older adults (sometimes called 'inflammaging') is linked to frailty, comorbidities, and hospitalization. It improves with resistance exercise, an anti-inflammatory diet, weight management, and control of conditions such as diabetes and hypertension. The nurse coordinates with physical therapy and dietitians rather than relying on long-term medications.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation in older adults responds to resistance training, diet, and control of comorbidities.
questions.hintContent: Recall the modifiable risk factors for chronic inflammation and the members of the interprofessional team who address them.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it treats the cause of chronic inflammation safely in an older adult.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Independent Interventions · Evaluating Cellulitis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with cellulitis of the forearm has received IV antibiotics for 48 hours. On admission, the nurse outlined the erythema with a skin marker. Which finding indicates that treatment is effective?
options: Erythema has receded inside the marked border
Temperature has increased from 37.8 °C to 38.4 °C (100.0 °F to 101.1 °F)
Erythema now extends 2 cm past the marked border
A new fluctuant area has developed in the center of the redness
optionRationales: Correct. Redness that has pulled back inside the marked line shows the local inflammation is resolving.
Incorrect. A rising temperature indicates worsening systemic inflammation.
Incorrect. Spreading erythema indicates worsening infection.
Incorrect. A fluctuant area suggests abscess formation that may need drainage.
questions.rationale: Marking the border of erythema provides an objective way to compare findings over time. Redness receding within the line, along with decreasing pain, swelling, temperature, and WBC, shows a positive response to antibiotics. Spreading redness, rising fever, or a new fluctuant area requires notification of the provider.
questions.takeaway: Redness shrinking inside the marked border = cellulitis is responding.
questions.hintContent: Recall the purpose of marking the border of erythema in skin infections.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide what an objective comparison with the admission baseline should show if the antibiotics are working, then test each option against it.
